sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation: The Masquerade of Neck Swelling
sections.description: This section details the patient's initial presentation, emphasizing the deceptive nature of the symptoms where dermatomyositis mimicked life-threatening conditions like Ludwig's angina or idiopathic angioedema. It guides the reader through the diagnostic pivot points where standard infectious and allergic workups failed, leading to the recognition of subtle cutaneous and neurological clues.
subtopics: Initial Emergency Department assessment: Differentiating between deep neck space infection and inflammatory edema
Red flags in 'idiopathic' angioedema: Lack of response to standard therapies and atypical distribution
Physical examination nuances: Identifying subtle signs often missed, including periungual erythema, nailfold microhemorrhages, and proximal muscle weakness
The role of dysphagia as an early indicator of bulbar involvement in inflammatory myopathies

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning: From CK Elevation to Autoantibody Specificity
sections.description: This section breaks down the stepwise investigative process used to confirm the diagnosis. It explains why Creatine Kinase (CK) was prioritized despite the primary complaint being neck swelling, interprets the specific utility of myositis-specific antibodies (specifically Anti-SAE1), and outlines how advanced imaging distinguished muscle inflammation from neoplasm or infection.
subtopics: The pivotal role of Creatine Kinase (CK) elevation (>16,000 U/L) in redirecting the differential diagnosis away from ENT pathology
Interpretation of serological profiles: Distinguishing Anti-SAE1 positivity from other myositis antibodies (Jo-1, Mi-2, TIF1-gamma)
Imaging modalities: Utilizing MRI for muscle specificity versus PET/CT for ruling out occult malignancy
Exclusion criteria: Why normal C3/C4 levels and negative infectious screens ruled out hereditary/acquired angioedema and sepsis

sections.description: Focusing on the underlying biological mechanisms, this section connects the clinical phenotype to cellular pathology. It explains how complement-mediated microvascular injury leads to perifascicular atrophy and subcutaneous edema, specifically addressing why Anti-SAE1 positive cases may present with unique features like pseudoangioedema without classic rashes.
subtopics: Mechanism of Dermatomyositis: Complement-mediated endothelial injury leading to ischemia and perifascicular atrophy
Role of Anti-SAE1 antibodies: Understanding their targeting of SUMO activating enzymes and correlation with dysphagia/lung disease
Histopathological hallmarks: Interpreting muscle biopsy findings including necrotic fibers, perimysial inflammation, and C5b-9 deposition
Pathogenesis of Pseudoangioedema: How muscle inflammation mimics true histaminergic or bradykinin-mediated swelling
